narrative_story:
# The Collectors

## I.

The newspapers reached the ceiling in columns so precise they looked structural, as though removing one would bring the hallway down. Mara turned sideways to pass between them—left shoulder leading, right arm trailing, a motion so practiced it had become her body's default orientation even in open spaces. She ran her fingers along the spines of the stacks the way other people touch banisters. Tuesday, March 12, 1996: hailstorm in Amarillo. Friday, September 3, 2004: Hurricane Frances makes landfall. Wednesday, December 26, 2018: freezing rain advisory, Cuyahoga County. Every paper organized by atmospheric catastrophe, subcategorized by precipitation type, cross-referenced in a spiral notebook she kept in her back pocket. The notebook was volume forty-seven. Volumes one through forty-six filled an entire closet she entered only when her breathing required it—when the anxiety thinned and the closet's density reminded her lungs how to work.

She reached the kitchen. Counters invisible beneath canned goods arranged by expiration date. She opened the refrigerator: Tupperware towers, each labeled with contents and the date of storage in her cramped handwriting. She wasn't hungry. She hadn't opened most of these in months. She closed the door and checked the seal twice, then three times, then stood with her palm flat against the refrigerator's face as though taking its pulse.

The mail was on the floor beneath the slot. She'd stopped using the mailbox outside in 2011 after a neighbor stole a circular. She dropped to her knees and sorted: junk, junk, bill, junk, coupon book she would clip and file and never use, and—

A white envelope. Hand-addressed. No return. The handwriting slanted left.

She held it for a long time before opening it. Then she added it to the stack beside the door, the one labeled URGENT—UNRESOLVED, which contained six hundred and fourteen items and had not been resolved once.

Then she picked it back up and tore it open.

---

The lighter was a cheap Bic, blue, nearly full. It belonged to a woman named Cassandra or Cassidy—Dev hadn't been listening when she introduced herself—who had set it on the bar beside her gin and tonic at the quarterly donor mixer for the Reinhardt Foundation, where Dev was a mid-level program officer responsible for evaluating grant applications in the arts. He was good at his job. His performance reviews used words like *meticulous* and *detail-oriented*. His supervisor had once called him the most trustworthy person in the office, which Dev had received with a smile that felt like a splinter working its way under a nail.

His hand moved. This was the part he'd stopped trying to narrate to himself, the part where intention and action uncoupled like train cars, the front half of his brain rolling on while the rear half detached and did what it was going to do regardless. His fingers closed around the Bic. His thumb tested the wheel—the faintest rasp of flint beneath the noise of the party—and then the lighter was in his jacket pocket, nestled against a stolen ballpoint pen, a stolen binder clip, and a stolen button that had been sitting loose on a conference table in the morning meeting.

He did not smoke. He did not need a pen—three sat in his breast pocket. The binder clip would end up in the drawer in his apartment that he opened only to add, never to retrieve, and the button matched no garment he owned or would ever own. Each item was valueless. Each theft was infrared: invisible to every spectrum of attention except his own.

He excused himself from the conversation and went to the bathroom and looked at the lighter under the fluorescent light and felt the brief, perfect silence that came after. Five seconds, maybe six. The noise coming back in was always the worst part.

At home, he found the envelope propped against his door. Hand-addressed. No return. Left-slanting script. He picked it up with the automatic, unthinking acquisitiveness with which he touched all objects left unattended, and the motion disgusted him because he couldn't tell if he was *receiving* mail or *taking* it.

---

Jules had a system. She'd built it across fifteen years and four cities and it ran with the precision of a Swiss movement, each gear engaging the next in a sequence so smooth it could be performed in a cocktail dress while carrying on a conversation about Medicaid reimbursement rates with the deputy director of a nonprofit whose annual gala she had organized, catered, and personally overseen the floral arrangements for, because Jules was a woman who managed things for other people with a competence so total that no one—not the deputy director, not the waitstaff, not the woman who'd hired her—ever looked closely enough to see what she managed about herself.

Two a.m. The restaurant's employee bathroom, which she'd chosen over the guest facilities because the lock was stronger. She knelt on tiles she'd ensured that morning were professionally cleaned. Her knees found the position—center of the second tile from the base—through muscle memory. Her left hand gathered her hair. Her right hand, the working hand, she held momentarily still.

The mascara would survive. It was Lancôme, waterproof, and she'd tested it. Her lipstick she'd already blotted to a stain. The dress was Diane von Furstenberg, black, and would show nothing. She had calculated the angle of lean that would protect the neckline. She had considered, rejected, and reconsidered a towel across her lap but decided the towel introduced variables: where to dispose of it, how to explain its absence from the rack.

The system engaged.

After, she stood, rinsed, checked herself in the mirror. Membrane intact. Surface holding. She smiled at her reflection with a warmth so practiced it could have raised funds for the American Cancer Society. Then she rejoined the party, and the deputy director told her everything had been perfect, *really just perfect*, and Jules thanked her and meant it in a way that was true and also the most elaborate lie she'd ever told, because the *perfection* the woman praised was the shell, and the shell was the sickness, and the sickness was the only thing that let the shell exist.

The envelope was in her apartment mailbox. She saw the handwriting and did not recognize it and felt her stomach clench, though her stomach clenching meant nothing diagnostic—her stomach clenched at everything now—and she opened it standing in the lobby in heels, mascara intact, and read it twice, and the second time her hands were shaking through no system she had built.

---

"—and my mother used to take me to this lake, this tiny glacial lake in northern Minnesota where the water was so clear you could see the bottom even at the center. You'd think that would make it less frightening, right? That transparency would equal safety? But it was the opposite. Because you could *see* how deep it was. You could see the rocks on the bottom sixty feet down and they looked close enough to touch and then you'd dive and they'd keep receding and you'd realize the clarity was a trick—the water had been showing you what was there the whole time, but it had also been lying about the distance."

Dr. Elaine Portman, licensed clinical psychologist, leaned forward by a degree that her training materials would have called *engaged presence*. "That's a powerful image, Toni."

"She drowned there. My mother."

"You've never mentioned that."

"I wasn't ready."

Dr. Portman's pen moved. Toni watched the pen and felt the warm, liquid satisfaction of a story landing precisely where she'd aimed it. The detail about the glacial lake she'd taken from a nature documentary. The drowning she'd borrowed from a novel she'd read in college and partially forgotten, which meant the details that survived—the clarity, the depth, the lying transparency—had composted in her memory until they felt like her own. Her mother was alive and lived in Scottsdale and had never visited a glacial lake and they spoke, if you could call it that, on major holidays with the television on.

The session ended. Toni drove home. She had told Dr. Portman, across forty-seven sessions, a version of her childhood that was architecturally magnificent: load-bearing tragedies positioned at precise intervals, each supporting the next, the whole structure plausible and internally consistent and almost entirely fabricated. Toni could not remember when the fabrication had started. She thought, sometimes, that it preceded language—that she'd been lying with her face before she had words to lie with. The question she could not answer and had never asked aloud was whether the *almost* in *almost entirely fabricated* referred to one true element or to none, whether there was a foundation under the architecture or just more architecture all the way down.

The letter was under her apartment door. Hand-addressed. No return.

She read it. She sat on her bed. She rehearsed three possible reactions—alarm, indifference, sardonic amusement—and settled on a fourth, which was a composite of the first three and looked, to an outside observer, like a woman calmly processing shocking news, when in fact it was a woman performing the act of calmly processing shocking news so convincingly that the performance replaced the processing entirely.

The white envelope sat on her nightstand. Identical. That was the part she couldn't manage by herself—the knowledge that three other envelopes existed, addressed to three other people who'd remember what was true.

---

## II.

*I watched what you four did to him that summer. I know where you buried it. Be at Camp Alder by midnight Friday or I send everything—photos, the item, my sworn testimony—to each of your employers, spouses, and parole officers.*

Toni read it for the eleventh time at a rest stop outside Sandusky. The "him" she had not thought about in seven years. The "it" she had not thought about in seven years. The specifics of both she had overwritten so many times with alternate versions—told to therapists, to partners, to herself at three in the morning when the original memory surfaced with its ugly contours—that seeking the original now was like looking for a painting beneath seventeen coats of primer. She knew it was under there. She knew the shape. She could not access the color.

*Parole officers.* Plural or singular? Dev, she assumed. Dev had been caught eventually—everyone who steals gets caught, and the fact that he stole useless objects wouldn't have mattered to whatever judge processed the misdemeanor. Or maybe it hadn't been a misdemeanor. She realized she didn't know anything about their lives and that this was by design: the four of them had severed contact with the efficiency of surgeons who understood that the tissue connecting them was malignant.

She started the car. She told herself she was going because the leverage was real. She told herself she was going because the risk to her constructed life—a life built on stories that required no witnesses to contradict them—was existential. She told herself three other reasons, each plausible, each partially true, and the act of layering reasons felt so familiar that she stopped at a fourth and drove.

---

Mara arrived at 9:47 p.m., two hours and thirteen minutes before the deadline. The drive from Cleveland had taken four hours because she'd packed the car the way she packed everything—comprehensively, categorically, against every conceivable contingency—and the weight had limited her to sixty-two miles per hour on the highway. The trunk held: bolt cutters, two socket wrench sets, a portable generator (non-functional, but she'd been meaning to repair it since 2016 and the trip felt like as good an occasion as any), eleven flashlights (three LED, four incandescent, two hand-crank, two item-unclear-but-cylindrical-and-therefore-provisionally-classified-as-flashlights), waterproof matches, a tarp, four tarps, a sleeping bag rated to negative forty, a second sleeping bag she didn't remember owning, an emergency radio, sixty-four batteries in mixed sizes, a first-aid kit, a second first-aid kit, canned soup (twelve units, assorted), a manual can opener, an electric can opener, a camp stove, two gallons of water, a sewing kit, and the forty-seventh spiral notebook, because weather could happen anywhere and needed to be recorded.

Camp Alder's gate was chained. The chain was new—someone had been here recently—and the padlock was commercial grade. Mara retrieved the bolt cutters from between the socket wrench sets and cut the chain with a clean stroke that surprised her. The metal fell away. The gate swung inward. The road beyond was unpaved and overgrown, and her headlights caught the shapes of cabins in the trees, and in her chest something opened that she did not have a filing system for.

She parked in the main circle and turned off the engine and sat. She'd come early the way she always came early, the way she kept things—not because of the thing itself but because letting go of the option, even the option of arrival, felt like a small death she wasn't willing to practice. Being first meant no one could start without her. Being first meant she hadn't missed anything. Being first meant the two hours and thirteen minutes before midnight were hers to hold.

---

Dev stopped four times between Columbus and the camp. At the first gas station he stole a pair of sunglasses from a spinning rack near the register—cheap plastic, green-tinted lenses. At the second he stole a pack of gum. At the third, a tire pressure gauge. At the fourth, another pair of sunglasses, these ones tortoiseshell, which he put on over the green ones and then removed both because the cumulative distortion made the road look like it was breathing.

He knew what he was doing. That was the part people misunderstood—friends, the therapist he'd seen twice before quitting, the public defender who'd argued (successfully, barely) that the objects' worthlessness indicated a compulsion rather than criminal intent. They assumed the behavior was unconscious. It wasn't. He felt every theft the way an addict feels a needle: the approach, the puncture, the flood, the quiet, the shame. The sequence was identical every time. He had mapped it. He had written it down. Mapping and writing did not produce cessation. They produced only a more articulate thief.

The stolen objects accrued in his pockets like sediment. Six items across four stops, and now his jacket was asymmetrical with the weight of things he didn't need, and his hands were steady in a way they hadn't been since the letter arrived, and the steadiness was the drug and the drug was the problem and the problem was the only solution he'd found to the other problem—the original one—which sat somewhere behind his ribs like a stone he'd swallowed at fourteen and never passed.

He arrived at 11:16 p.m. Mara's car, absurdly overloaded, was already in the circle. The gate hung open. He parked and sat in the dark and put his hand in his pocket and closed his fingers around the tire pressure gauge and felt his pulse slow and hated every chamber of his heart for slowing.

---

Jules had not eaten in thirty-six hours. This was not, by her accounting, unusual. Thirty-six hours was within parameters. She could function at thirty-six hours—could drive, could think, could carry on the kind of conversation that required surface fluency but not depth. Forty-eight hours was where the perceptual distortions began, the faint shimmer at the edge of objects, and she was calibrated to land well below forty-eight. She'd had water. She'd had black coffee. Her body was an instrument she knew the tolerances of, and she was operating within spec.

The drive from Chicago was long enough that she'd had to stop for gas twice and the smell of the convenience store both times—the rotating hot dogs, the nacho cheese, the ambient sweetness of packaged pastry—had been a negotiation conducted entirely below the level of articulate thought. Her body wanted. Her body was an idiot. She managed the wanting the way she managed events: with schedules, contingencies, and a refusal to acknowledge that the thing being managed was, in fact, in control.

She arrived at 11:38 p.m. Two cars in the circle already. She recognized neither—people change their cars every few years the way they change their faces, gradually and then all at once—but she knew, from the way Mara's rear axle sagged, whose it was.

She parked. She checked her mirror. Mascara intact. She was not wearing lipstick—this was not a lipstick occasion—but she'd moisturized, and her skin looked human, and looking human was the baseline she maintained at all times because the alternative
